what: Alerting watches your metrics and wakes a human (a page) only when users are being hurt and someone must act. Everything less urgent becomes a ticket or a dashboard line.
like: Like a smoke alarm: it should ring for real fire, loudly and rarely. One that beeps at toast gets its battery pulled.
why: Problems are fixed in minutes instead of when a customer complains
Paging on SLO burn ties every page to real user pain
Grouping, routing and runbooks let one tired person handle a night shift calmly

nodes.t: Runbook|what to check, how to fix

steps.d: Rules watch what users feel - errors, latency, failed checks - not causes like high CPU. A cause gets a page only when it is certain and close, like a disk about to fill.
Burn rate is how fast you spend the error budget. Burn rate 1 spends it exactly over the SLO window; 14.4 spends 2% of a 30-day budget in one hour.
Fire only if both a long window (1 hour) and a short window (5 minutes, 1/12 of it) are burning. The long one proves it matters; the short one ends the alert quickly once fixed.
AI answers change run to run. Alert when a citation rate's confidence interval moves clearly below its baseline, not when one run misses. Per-series baselines beat one fixed threshold.
Alertmanager bundles related alerts into one message, mutes warnings while a matching critical fires (inhibition), and routes by labels: critical pages a person, warning opens a ticket.
Every page links a runbook: what the alert means, a dashboard, first checks and safe fixes. If the steps are robotic, automate them and delete the page.

numbers.l: burn over 1h (5m short window) pages: 2% budget spent
burn over 6h (30m short window) pages: 5% budget spent
burn over 3 days (6h short window) opens a ticket
short window length compared with the long window

choices.d: Page only for user-facing harm that needs action now. Slow budget burn, capacity trends and single failures go to tickets or a dashboard.
Start from the SRE workbook set: 14.4x over 1h and 6x over 6h page, 1x over 3 days tickets. Tune for your traffic; low-traffic services need minimum request counts.
group_by cluster and alertname so one outage is one message. Defaults: wait 30s to batch, 5m between updates, 4h before repeating.
Mute warnings when a critical alert with the same cluster is firing, and mute everything behind a downed dependency, so on-call sees the root symptom.
Static is clear and fine for SLOs. Per-series or seasonal baselines suit metrics with daily cycles or very different normal levels, but are harder to explain.

instead.why: Dashboards for slow trends and subcritical issues that should not page
After the page: trace one slow request to find the cause
Catch quality drops before release instead of alerting after
Let the system fix known failures itself so nobody gets paged

breaks.d: Too many pages, most needing no action, so people skim or ignore them.
breaks.see: Pages per shift rising, many acked and closed with no change
breaks.fix: Delete or demote non-actionable alerts, review paging load every week, page on SLO burn

breaks.d: One failure fires hundreds of alerts across services.
breaks.see: Phone buzzing nonstop, the real cause buried
breaks.fix: group_by and inhibition rules; alert on the user symptom at the edge

breaks.d: A value hovers near the line and fires and resolves again and again.
breaks.see: Same alert opening and closing many times an hour
breaks.fix: A for duration, multiwindow burn rates, or keep_firing_for

breaks.d: A sampled signal, like LLM citation checks, dips by chance.
breaks.see: Pages that clear on the next run with no change made
breaks.fix: Alert on confidence intervals over enough runs, compare to a per-series baseline

breaks.d: The alert never fires because the metric itself vanished.
breaks.see: Users report an outage, dashboards show gaps instead of red
breaks.fix: Alert on up == 0 and absent(), plus an always-firing heartbeat alert checked externally

say: I alert on symptoms users feel, measured as SLO burn rate, not on causes like CPU.
Using the SRE workbook pattern, I page when 14.4x burn shows over both 1 hour and 5 minutes, or 6x over 6 hours and 30 minutes, and open a ticket for 1x over 3 days.
Alertmanager groups related alerts, inhibits warnings under a critical one and routes by severity, and every page links a runbook.
For noisy signals like AI citation checks, I alert when the confidence interval moves below baseline, not on a single missed run.

followups.q: Why two windows instead of one?
followups.a: A long window alone is slow to reset after a fix; a short one alone is jumpy. Requiring both means the problem is big enough to matter and still happening now.
Burn rate 1 spends exactly the whole error budget over the SLO period, say 30 days. At 14.4 you would spend it in about two days, and one hour of it already uses 2% of the budget.

followups.q: How do you measure if alerting is good?
followups.a: Precision (how many alerts were real), recall (how many real problems alerted), detection time and reset time. Also track pages per shift and the share that needed action.

Static SLO-based alerts are easy to reason about and should carry paging. Adaptive baselines help for seasonal or per-customer metrics, often as warnings first, because unexplained model alerts erode trust.

today: The multiwindow multi-burn-rate pattern from the Google SRE workbook is now built into common tools; Grafana Cloud, for example, has a 2025 guide to setting it up for SLOs.

check.q: Which is the best paging signal?
check.a: Error budget burning fast for users
check.why: Pages should be about symptoms users feel. CPU and disk are causes, better as tickets or dashboards.

check.q: In the SRE workbook, what does burn rate 14.4 over 1 hour mean for a 30-day budget?
check.a: About 2% of the budget is spent
check.why: 14.4 x 1 hour / 720 hours = 2%. That is fast enough to wake someone.

check.q: A critical 'cluster down' alert fires. What stops 40 warnings from the same cluster paging too?
check.why: Inhibition mutes target alerts while a matching source alert is firing.

check.q: Your AI citation-rate check drops for one run then recovers. Best alerting design?
check.a: Alert when the confidence interval over many runs falls below baseline
d: Page on every single missed citation
Raise the static threshold to zero
check.why: LLM answers vary run to run, so judge a sample, not one result.
